title: Leap Year

rules: Div by 4 and not by 100 → leap.
remember.takeaway: When rules have exceptions-to-exceptions, encode them as one OR of ANDs.
whenToUse: Encoding a spec as one boolean expression

problemStatement: Given a year `y`, return whether it is a leap year. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, **except** century years (divisible by 100) which must also be divisible by 400.
understanding: Two rules interact: every 4th year is a leap year, but every 100th year is skipped, unless it is also a 400th year.

approaches.name: Boolean rule
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
The rule has an exception inside an exception: a year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, **except** centuries (divisible by 100), **unless** the century is also divisible by 400. The cleanest encoding is one boolean expression: `(y % 4 == 0 && y % 100 != 0) || (y % 400 == 0)`.

**Why this exact shape.** The first clause captures 'divisible by 4 but not a plain century'. The second clause, OR-ed in, re-admits the special centuries (2000, 2400) that are divisible by 400. Because the 400-rule is its own OR term, it cleanly overrides the 100-exception without nested conditionals.

**The classic gotcha: 1900 vs 2000.** 1900 is divisible by 100 but not 400, so it is *not* a leap year — many naive solutions that only check `% 4` get this wrong. 2000 is divisible by 400, so it *is*. These two years are the test the interviewer is really running.

Translating an English spec with nested exceptions into one OR-of-ANDs is the transferable skill here — it shows up again in date math, validation rules, and permission checks.

code.python:
def is_leap(y: int) -> bool:
    return (y % 4 == 0 and y % 100 != 0) or (y % 400 == 0)

hints: Start with the simple rule (divisible by 4), then layer the exceptions.
Centuries (÷100) are skipped — unless they're also ÷400.
Encode it as one OR of two ANDs; test it on 1900 and 2000.
approaches.insight: Getting the precedence right between the 100 and 400 rules is the whole test — 1900 vs 2000 is the classic gotcha.
approaches.complexityReasoning: three modulo checks at most — constant.

dryRun.intro: The two years that separate correct from naive solutions.

edgeCases.behavior: Divisible by 4, not a century → leap year (true).

pitfalls: Checking only `y % 4 == 0`, which wrongly marks 1900 as a leap year.
Getting the precedence of the 100 and 400 rules backwards.

commonMistakes: Returning `y % 4 == 0` only — wrongly marks 1900 as a leap year.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can translate a spec with an exception-to-an-exception into correct boolean logic.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Only testing divisibility by 4 and mishandling century years.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Call out 1900 (false) and 2000 (true) yourself as the boundary cases that validate the rule.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I assume the Gregorian calendar?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the 4/100/400 rule is Gregorian; pre-1582 dates would differ.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Only checking divisibility by 4
commonMistakesDetailed.why: It marks every century (1700, 1800, 1900) as a leap year, which is wrong unless they're also divisible by 400.
